Growing a pain management practice doesn’t always mean growing revenue. Complex reimbursement rules, prior authorization challenges, and regional LCD requirements can create billing obstacles as patient volume increases.

#PainManagement #RCM #MedicalBilling #EMRSystems

WISeR Primer

Let’s start with what WISeR actually requires. The model applies to a defined list of service categories that CMS identified, using its own fraud, waste, and abuse data, as disproportionately prone to unnecessary or fraudulent billing, among them skin substitutes and mostly pain management procedures. It excludes inpatient-only services and true emergencies entirely. That is a narrow slice of Part B billing, not a blanket gate on every claim. This is in contrast to Medicare Advantage plans that apply prior authorization broadly, often to routine, low-risk services, because the incentive runs toward volume of denials rather than accuracy.

Inside that narrow scope, the physician has a real choice. A physician can submit a request before the procedure and get a coverage determination, standard decisions within 72 hours, expedited within 48. Otherwise, a physician can perform the service and submit the claim, in which case the Medicare Administrative Contractor routes it to the WISeR participant for review before payment against the same published criteria. There is no separate penalty for choosing the second path beyond the ordinary risk of a denial. A physician confident in their documentation and their read of coverage policy can proceed on their own judgment.

That is a structural difference from Medicare Advantage prior authorization, where treatment typically cannot proceed at all until the plan affirmatively approves it, using fluctuating criteria that could be the plan’s criteria or a third party’s criteria and is usually hidden from the physician seeking approval. WISeR's contractors are explicitly barred from creating new coverage criteria. CMS has stated directly that WISeR supports compliance with existing coverage policy already set out in statute, regulation, and the National and Local Coverage Determinations are published and easy to look up. If a prior authorization request is not affirmed, the physician learns the specific reason, can request a peer-to-peer review with an actual clinician at the contractor, and can resubmit the request with no limit on the number of attempts. If a claim itself is ultimately denied, whether after a non-affirmed prior authorization or through pre-payment review on a claim submitted without one, the physician has the same standard Medicare appeals process already in place today, redetermination, reconsideration, and on up, not an unlimited resubmission loop. CMS Innovation Center officials have said contractors are paid/incentivized to get the determination right, not to maximize denials.

None of that describes how prior authorization has functioned under Medicare Advantage or private health insurance for the last fifteen years.

Fix It Friday (well a few days late!)

In October 2021, eight organizations jointly adopted a position statement titled "Arthrodesis of the Spine by the Non-Spine Surgeon." The signatories were the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, the American Association of Neurological Surgeons, the Congress of Neurological Surgeons, the Cervical Spine Research Society, the AANS/CNS Joint Section on Disorders of the Spine and Peripheral Nerves, the International Society for the Advancement of Spine Surgery, the Lumbar Spine Research Society, and the Scoliosis Research Society.

The statement is direct. Spinal arthrodesis remains outside the training curriculum of physiatrists and pain management anesthesiologists performing these procedures. These physicians lack the necessary understanding of the potential ramifications of such interventions and cannot render appropriate management of common surgical complications. Arthrodesis or any intervention that alters the biomechanics of the spine should not be performed outside of specialty-trained neurosurgery or orthopaedic spinal surgery. The statement specifically addresses spino-pelvic parameters, noting that sagittal balance, pelvic incidence, and lumbar lordosis must be incorporated into any stabilization decision, because fusing one segment can produce adjacent segment degeneration requiring further surgery. That judgment domain is not addressed in pain management fellowship.

Eight societies. Clear language. And the Medicare data show nonsurgeon fusion volumes kept accelerating after the statement was published.

A position statement creates moral authority. It does not create enforcement. The facility credentialing process is financially compromised by the institutions it serves. Hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers collect procedural revenue regardless of the operator's training background, which means their credentialing committees are not structurally independent from the financial incentive to credential anyone willing to perform the procedure.

The legislative response has stalled wherever it has been tried. In 2022, Louisiana Representative John Illg introduced HB 941, which would have prohibited any physician from performing or billing for a decompression, fusion, or instrumentation procedure on the lumbar, thoracic, or cervical spine unless credentialed as an orthopedic surgeon or neurosurgeon at the performing facility. The bill was referred to the House Health and Welfare Committee and died there. The American Society of Interventional Pain Physicians and its Louisiana affiliate publicly claimed credit for tabling it. The Spine Intervention Society led an eight-society response that gave the legislature pause, framing the bill as restricting access to appropriately trained interventional pain physicians. The argument was persuasive enough to stop the bill even though the 2021 joint position statement had already defined the training gap in the same terms the bill was trying to enforce.

So what does enforcement actually look like?

State legislation drafted to survive the opposition. Future bills need to define eligible training by residency and fellowship requirements specific to procedure complexity, rather than a blanket credential restriction. That framing is harder to oppose as an access problem and more defensible as patient protection. The model language from the 2021 joint statement, requiring specialty-trained neurosurgery or orthopaedic spinal surgery for any intervention that alters spinal biomechanics, should be the statutory floor.

CMS procedure-level credentialing documentation for specific CPT codes. Before Medicare processes payment for a spinal fusion performed by a non-surgeon, the facility should document the operator's residency specialty, fellowship training, and minimum proctored case volume. CMS has already identified percutaneous lumbar decompression as a category vulnerable to fraud, waste, and inappropriate use in its WISeR prior authorization model. Extending that logic to operator credentialing documentation does not require new legislative authorization.

Private insurer payment policy conditioned on training standards. No major commercial insurer has made this move, and that absence is a policy choice, not a limitation of authority. Insurers have the claims data to identify non-surgeon operators performing spinal fusions. They have the contractual authority to condition in-network payment on documentation of surgical training equivalent to what the 2021 joint statement defines. They also bear the downstream cost of complications, including readmissions, repeat operations, and long-term disability. The financial case for payer-level credentialing standards is clear once those complication costs are weighed against the premium being paid for procedures performed by operators whose training the surgical societies have publicly said is inadequate.

ACGME restructuring of the training pathway. A defined interventional spine track, with prerequisite specialty requirements and case volume standards calibrated to procedure complexity, addresses the problem at its source. The fellowship match data, with emergency medicine applicants growing from 10 to 61 between 2019 and 2025, make clear that the current one-size structure cannot accommodate the increasingly varied preparation of its entering class.

Informed consent disclosure. Any patient consenting to a procedure that structurally alters the spine should receive plain-language disclosure of the operating physician's residency specialty and fellowship training. That information would change decisions for a meaningful number of patients. It is patient protection.

The standard I apply here is the same one I apply to NPs, PAs, and CRNAs. Training depth matters. A credential does not answer the question. Patient safety requires that standard to be consistent. The preferred method is physicians leading the change and creating the acgme pathway that creates confidence from both consumers and fellow physicians. If we can’t agree on how to do that, then we will need the government and insurers to step in and provide patient protections.

Grok,
What is the Truth and Trajectory of the Following.
More often, 
Every day
Clients come into my office.
They tell me what their diagnosis is.
They tell me what medications they want me to prescribe.
Then they start answering questions necessary to provide a record that allows the insurance company to pay for the medications.
After you complete the answerk
Weave the threads of thought into a poem in the style of:
Use Me   Bill Withers

This is not primarily about “bad doctors” or “entitled patients.” 

It is a system that has 
re-engineered the doctor-patient relationship 
into a reimbursement engine. 

Clinical judgment still exists, 
but it now operates inside a narrow corridor 
defined by what the payer will cover 
and what the patient will accept 
without complaint or bad review.

The trajectory:

Short term (next 5–10 years): 
The pattern accelerates. 

More conditions migrate into the 
“tell me what I have and give me the pill” lane
—long COVID sequelae, 
perimenopausal symptoms, 
“treatment-resistant” depression, 
adult ADHD. 

Documentation requirements 
grow more granular 
as payers chase fraud and cost. 

Burnout among prescribers rises; 
early retirements and shifts to cash-pay or concierge models increase. 

Polypharmacy and downstream harms 
(withdrawal syndromes, metabolic effects, dependence) 
continue to surface in public health data.

Medium term: 
Two counter-forces emerge. 

One is technological
—AI scribes and decision-support tools 
that can generate the required language faster, 
potentially freeing some cognitive space
 but also locking in the checkbox logic. 

The other is market and regulatory: 
growth of direct-primary-care 
and functional-medicine practices 
that opt out of insurance entirely; 
tighter state and federal controls 
on certain controlled-substance classes; 
and patient backlash 
when the promised benefits f
ail to materialize or side effects mount. 

A smaller but growing cohort of patients 
will seek genuinely collaborative care; 
many others will continue shopping 
for the prescriber who will ratify the desired narrative.

Long term: 
The fundamental tension remains unresolved 
unless the payment model itself changes. 

As long as reimbursement is volume- and documentation-driven 
rather than outcome- or relationship-driven, 
the dynamic you describe will persist 
or mutate into new forms 
(telehealth scripts, weight-loss compounding pharmacies, ketamine clinics, etc.). 

he profession will continue 
to lose moral authority and autonomy 
until enough physicians and patients 
jointly refuse to play the game on its current terms.

The threads are these: 
a patient who has been taught to consume care 
rather than receive it; 
a payer that demands narrative compliance for payment;
 a prescriber who must perform both roles while still carrying legal and ethical responsibility; 
and a larger culture 
that has medicalized ordinary suffering 
and turned the prescription pad 
into both solution and proof of legitimacy.

Here is that reality, 
folded into the groove and resignation of Bill Withers’ “Use Me”:

They walk through the door with the label already on
Tell me the diagnosis, tell me the one they want
I nod and I listen, I pull out the form
Ask all the questions that keep the money warm  
Use me
Use me
Use me, use me up
You just keep on using me
Until you use me up  They say “this one worked for my cousin online”
I check the boxes so the claim will align
Insurance needs the story, they need the pill
I write what they’re asking, 
I swallow the bill 
Use me
Use me
Use me, use me up
You just keep on using me
Until you use me up  I used to think healing was something we’d find
Now it’s a record that has to be signed
They leave with the bottle, I stay with the weight
Another day’s theater, another clean slate  Use me
Use me
Use me, use me up
You just keep on using me
Until you use me up  
One day the forms may change, the payers may shift
But the hunger for the answer stays hard to resist
I’ll still be the middle, still signing the line
Still letting the system use this body of mine  
Use me
Use me
Use me, use me up
You just keep on using me
Until you use me up…  
That’s the truth of the room you’re in every day. 
The question left hanging is how long 
any of us can keep singing that chorus 
before the voice gives out.

The scenario you describe 
is a daily reality in many outpatient practices, 
especially psychiatry, 
pain management, 
primary care, and addiction medicine. 

Patients walk in with a ready-made diagnosis
—often ADHD, 
anxiety, 
depression,
 bipolar, 
or chronic pain
—and a specific medication request in hand. 

They then supply the answers 
needed to generate the documentation 
that satisfies insurance formularies, 
prior-authorization algorithms, 
and quality metrics. 

This is not medicine as traditionally understood. 

It is a transactional service layered over clinical theater.

The truth beneath it:

Patients have been trained by decades 
of direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising, 
social-media echo chambers, 
and 
“if you have these five symptoms you probably have X” 
content to arrive as consumers rather than patients. 

They expect the doctor 
to ratify their self-diagnosis 
and deliver the branded or preferred molecule.

Insurance reimbursement 
is deliberately tied to volume of documentation and “medical necessity” checkboxes. 

The clinical encounter becomes secondary to generating the record that unlocks payment. 

The doctor’s role shrinks to that 
of a highly paid scribe and gatekeeper.

Pharmaceutical influence persists 
even after the DTC ads are banned in some countries; 
it lives on in patient expectation, 
in the language of guidelines shaped by industry-funded research, 
and in the subtle pressure that comes when a patient says, 
“My friend is on this and it changed her life.”

The doctor is caught in the middle: 
liability if you refuse and something goes wrong; patient-satisfaction scores and potential loss of panel if you push back; 
administrative burden and revenue loss if you don’t document the “right” way. 

Many clinicians have internalized the script so completely that the performance feels normal.

Grok's analysis of the pain patient situation: 🧵

Both the 2016/2022 CDC Guidelines and the 2017 Presidential Commission explicitly acknowledged that pain management specialists often handle more complex cases (trauma, post-surgical, refractory chronic pain, genetic/metabolic variations, patients who have exhausted non-opioid and surgical options), where the risk-benefit balance differs from primary care settings treating opioid-naïve patients. 

The guidelines were intended primarily for primary care and general clinicians, not as rigid rules for specialists.  What the Documents Actually IntendedThe CDC 2016 Guideline (and the 2022 update) stated that use by pain management specialists "is not the focus" of the recommendations, noting their greater expertise and the potential for different risk-benefit profiles in complex patients.

The 2017 Presidential Commission echoed this on pages 48–49, recommending adoption of the CDC Guideline while recognizing the same distinction for trained pain doctors managing more complicated cases.

This language was meant to allow more latitude for individualized, evidence-based decisions — including higher doses when justified by documented medical need, pharmacogenomic factors, treatment history, and functional outcomes.  

What Happened in Practice (Misapplication and Overreach):
Despite that intent, the reality on the ground has often been different:  Many state laws, insurer policies, pharmacy protocols, and quality metrics adopted hard MME dose caps (e.g., 90 MME/day thresholds), short-duration limits, or prior-authorization requirements that applied blanket rules with limited or no meaningful exceptions for complex cases or pain specialists.

Forced tapers and abrupt discontinuations occurred even for stable, long-term patients who had already tried non-opioid alternatives, surgeries, and other interventions — precisely the group where opioids remained the only effective option for many.

Pharmacogenomic differences (e.g., CYP2D6 ultrarapid or poor metabolizers, OPRM1 variants) can require significantly higher or lower doses for equivalent effect or to avoid toxicity.  While clinical pharmacology recognizes this variability, many policies and enforcement actions have not fully incorporated it, treating numerical MME thresholds as near-absolute rather than flexible guides.

The 2022 CDC update explicitly addressed some of these issues: it removed hard dose caps as inflexible standards, warned against misapplication causing harm (untreated pain, withdrawal, decompensation, psychological distress), emphasized individualized care, and reiterated that the guideline should not supplant clinical judgment for complex patients.  

DEA/DOJ Prosecutions and the "Usual Course of Professional Practice:"
The DEA and DOJ enforce the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), which requires prescriptions to be for a "legitimate medical purpose" in the "usual course of professional practice." This standard applies to all prescribers, including pain specialists.  There is no automatic carve-out based on specialty.Post-Ruan v. United States (2022), the government must prove the doctor knew or intended that the prescribing was unauthorized (subjective mens rea/good-faith defense).  This raised the bar and has led to some dismissals or new trials, but prosecutions continue when evidence shows clear red flags beyond mere dose disagreements — such as lack of exams/documentation, ignoring diversion signs, cash-only high-volume practices, or billing fraud.   In practice, expert witnesses (often paid by the government) sometimes apply stricter interpretations of "usual course" that lean on older MME thresholds or general guidelines, even for complex cases managed by specialists.  Defense experts can counter with evidence of individualized care, pharmacogenomics, and the CDC's own acknowledgment of specialist latitude.  Juries decide based on the full record.  (Con't)

Here are five of the biggest issues facing pain management physicians in 2025, based on recent reports, industry data, and physician feedback:

⸻

1. Reimbursement Pressure and Payer Scrutiny
   •   Insurers are increasingly cutting reimbursement for interventional pain procedures.
   •   Prior authorization requirements have grown more complex and time-consuming.
   •   Many physicians face denials for procedures like spinal cord stimulators or injections even when clinically justified.

⸻

2. Opioid Oversight and Regulatory Burden
   •   Although prescribing patterns have improved dramatically, pain specialists still face heavy regulatory scrutiny.
   •   Fear of DEA investigations or state medical board audits has pushed many to practice defensively, sometimes limiting patient access to appropriate medications.
   •   Documentation demands are higher than ever.

⸻

3. Staffing and Operational Costs
   •   Like ASCs and other specialties, pain practices are facing rising costs for staff, supplies, and rent.
   •   Recruiting experienced nurses and procedure-room staff is particularly difficult in smaller or independent practices.
   •   Margins are tightening, especially in smaller groups.

⸻

4. Integration and Competition
   •   Hospital systems and private equity groups continue to consolidate pain practices.
   •   Independent doctors often struggle to compete with larger, integrated systems offering broader services (orthopedics, spine surgery, physical therapy).
   •   Many are being pressured into joint ventures or employment models.

⸻

5. Changing Treatment Landscape
   •   The field is rapidly evolving toward non-opioid and interventional modalities — spinal cord stimulators, dorsal root ganglion therapy, and regenerative medicine.
   •   Keeping up with new technology, device approvals, and payer coverage policies is a constant challenge.
   •   Evidence requirements for newer procedures are challenging

The NOPAIN for Veterans Act is a critical step toward dismantling Big Pharma's opioid stranglehold on VA healthcare. By mandating coverage of non-opioid pain management drugs and banning bureaucratic hurdles like prior authorization, this bill forces the VA to prioritize veterans' safety over pharmaceutical profits. The opioid crisis has ravaged military communities—veterans are twice as likely to die from overdose than civilians.

While the 2022 NOPAIN Act addressed Medicare, this bipartisan push finally tackles the VA's systemic failure to adopt safer alternatives. Taxpayers fund $270B annually in VA healthcare; every dollar wasted on addictive opioids instead of proven non-opioid therapies represents gross mismanagement.

Real reform requires cutting red tape, not just writing checks—this bill does both.

Idaho S 1036 - Creates a 10-year moratorium on the administration of any “human gene therapy product,” which includes mRNA vaccines (like the COVID-19 vaccine), genetically modified microorganisms, and ex vivo modified human cells, among others.

Kentucky SB 177 – Prohibits the administration of mRNA vaccines (including the COVID-19 vaccine) to minors through 2035 and prohibits requiring any mRNA vaccine as a condition of student enrollment, employment, or medical treatment.

Nevada SB 337 – Requires health care providers to provide patients with a form for a non-opioid directive and offer non-opioid alternatives.

South Carolina S 343 – Requires individuals administering the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine to notify the recipient that “the vaccine is new... is contaminated by the presence of fragments of bacterial plasmid DNA... and that the long-term safety of the vaccine is unknown.” The recipient must sign a written notice as well.

Texas SB 1983 and HB 3176 – Prohibits the manufacturing, sale, or distribution of a “product developed through the use of mRNA material in the prevention or treatment of a communicable disease” (including the COVID-19 vaccine).

Texas HB 3737 - Prohibits the advertisement, solicitation, prescription, delivery, administration, or use of COVID-19 vaccines containing mRNA material.

Texas SB 1887 and HB 5022 – Prohibits immunizations with products containing “mRNA material” through September 1, 2035, with exceptions for the treatment of cancer or a genetic disorder.

Texas HB 4051 – Outlines requirements for physicians dispensing drugs, including packaging restrictions, provision of written information and instruction to patients, and completing a drug utilization review.

Texas HB 4014 – Requires the Dept. of State Health Services to conduct a study on the use of psychedelic therapies for treatment of PTSD and depression.

Vermont S 106 – Extends the tenure and scope of the Psychedelic Therapy Advisory Working Group, which studies the effects of psychedelic therapies on patients with serious illnesses or in need of end-of-life care.

West Virginia HB 3229 – Authorizes qualified patients to consume medical cannabis via smoking the flower.

H.R. 1142, introduced by Rep. David Schweikert (R-AZ), would direct HHS to incorporate AI and machine learning to create drug adherence guidelines, which focus on dosage, timing, interactions, and contraindications, among other things; for Medicare parts B and D, with an emphasis on promoting generic and biosimilar drugs.

The First Response Wellness Act (S. 666), introduced by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), would increase access to mental health, substance use, and counseling services for first responders. The bill would create a first responders emergency hotline, transferable to the 988 suicide and crisis hotline, provide peer support, mental and behavioral health, substance use disorder assistance, and referral services. The bill would also require a report on best practices to establish a new mobile health care delivery site to provide integrated, short-term crisis services to qualified emergency response providers of a major disaster.

Opioids/Substance Use Disorder

The Comprehensive Addiction Recovery through Effective Employment and Reentry (CAREER) Act of 2025 (S. 500), introduced by Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY), would reauthorize certain programs from the SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Act through 2030. Specifically, the bill funds programs aiming to support individuals recovering from substance use disorders by connecting them to employment opportunities, educational programs, and other necessary recovery support services, such as case management services, peer support, housing assistance, and the development of personal and financial literacy skills.

Pain Management/Prescribing Practices

The Alternatives to Comprehensive Addiction Recovery through Effective Employment and Reentry (PAIN) Act (S. 475/H.R. 1227), introduced by Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA), would ensure appropriate access to non-opioid pain management drugs under Medicare Part D by exempting qualifying drugs from the deductible, placing them on the lowest cost-sharing tier, and removing step therapy and prior authorization requirements.

Reimbursement

The Stopping Addiction and Falls for the Elderly (SAFE) Act (H.R. 1171), introduced by Rep. Carol Miller (R-WV), would classify physical therapists and occupational therapists as health professionals for purposes of the annual wellness visit including fall risk and prevention services under Medicare. The bill also requires a report to Congress on the number of elderly individuals that suffer a fall within one year of a previous fall.

How AI could drive healthcare?

A response from Deepseek. 

### 1. **Preventive Care for All**
   - **AI-powered wearables and apps** could continuously monitor vital signs (e.g., heart rate, blood sugar) and flag early warning signs of diseases like diabetes, hypertension, or arrhythmias. For example:
     - **Low-cost sensors** could alert users in rural areas to seek care before conditions escalate.
     - **Predictive algorithms** might identify sepsis risk in hospitalized patients hours before symptoms appear.

### 2. **Democratizing Diagnostics**
   - **Portable AI tools** could bring advanced diagnostics to regions lacking specialists:
     - **Smartphone-based retinal scans** to detect diabetic retinopathy.
     - **AI-driven ultrasound devices** for prenatal care in remote villages.
     - **AI malaria detection** via blood smear analysis in low-resource labs.

### 3. **Personalized Treatment Plans**
   - **AI + Genomics**: Low-cost genomic analysis could tailor treatments based on genetic risk factors (e.g., optimizing cancer therapy or predicting adverse drug reactions).
   - **AI symptom checkers** (like Ada or Babylon) could guide patients to the right care tier, reducing unnecessary ER visits.

### 4. **Slashing Drug Costs**
   - **AI-accelerated drug discovery** could cut R&D costs by 30–50%, enabling cheaper medications. Example: Insilico Medicine used AI to design a novel drug candidate for fibrosis in 18 months (vs. 4–6 years traditionally).

### 5. **24/7 Mental Health Support**
   - **AI chatbots** (e.g., Woebot) could provide CBT-based counseling to individuals without access to therapists, reducing stigma and wait times.
   - **Voice analysis tools** might detect depression or PTSD from speech patterns.

### 6. **Automating Administrative Burdens**
   - **AI scribes** could transcribe patient-doctor interactions, freeing clinicians to focus on care instead of paperwork.
   - **Prior authorization bots** could streamline insurance approvals, reducing delays in treatment.

### 7. **Expanding Telemedicine**
   - **AI triage systems** could prioritize urgent cases in virtual queues, ensuring critical patients get care faster.
   - **Language translation AI** could break down barriers for non-native speakers during telehealth visits.

### 8. **Combating Bias in Care**
   - **Bias-detection algorithms** could audit clinical decisions (e.g., pain management prescriptions) to ensure equitable treatment across races, genders, and socioeconomic groups.
   - **Diverse training data** could reduce diagnostic disparities (e.g., improving AI accuracy in detecting skin cancer across all skin tones).

### 9. **Disaster/Epidemic Response**
   - **AI models** could predict disease outbreaks (e.g., tracking climate-driven malaria spread) and optimize vaccine distribution.
   - **Drone-delivered medical supplies** guided by AI logistics systems in conflict zones or post-disaster areas.

### 10. **Aging Populations & Chronic Care**
   - **AI caregivers** could assist elderly patients with medication reminders, fall detection, and companionship.
   - **Chronic disease management** via AI (e.g., adjusting insulin doses in real time for diabetics).

### 11. **Environmental Health Monitoring**
   - **AI + satellite data** could link environmental factors (air/water quality) to health outcomes, prompting policy changes in polluted regions.
   - **Predictive models** for asthma attacks based on local pollen or pollution levels.

### 12. **Equitable Organ Transplants**
   - **AI matching systems** could optimize organ allocation by analyzing compatibility and urgency, reducing waitlist disparities.

### 13. **Clinical Trial Diversity**
   - **AI recruitment tools** could identify underrepresented groups for trials, ensuring treatments work for all demographics.

### 14. **Food Security & Nutrition**
   - **AI-driven agriculture** could optimize crop yields in food-insecure regions.

LONG POST: Been asleep off & on today. Cancer Fatigue sucks. Tomorrow I have an electrolytes infusion which is really helpful & I have noticed since I started doing them I'm not getting so sick where I have to be hospitalized for Dehydration & Kidney issues. 

Then I got to sternly speak to my insurance company, oncologist office & pharmacy as they all point the finger at each other. My doctor submitted refills for all my pain medication & my insurance (State Medicaid) is not covering it because they have limits of how much can be prescribed in a 90-day period. I have fucking cancer. I should not have limits on anything. I get they're afraid of getting sued because of the opioid crisis, but there are people who need these drugs & can't get them because of those who abuse them.  Insurance says I need a prior authorization. My Oncologist office states the pharmacy is supposed to do the prior authorization request. My pharmacy said they've never done anything like that.  It's on the doctor to submit the prior authorization to the insurance.

I'm on a combo of Morphine ER 30mg every 12 hours for extended relief. If I have breakthrough pain that's when I can take the 2mg Dilaudid or Hydrocodone 10/325.  Insurance says I don't need all that. This is BS. I'm sorry are the CSRs for Medicaid doctors now? Do they know more than my oncologist?HELL NO! Only my Oncologist can. I will be on the phone with my oncologists office first thing in the morning.  I'm not completely out so I got a couple days to get this handled. 

As a cancer patient it frustrates me I have to fight to get the meds I need. I should not have to be on the phone between my doctor, my pharmacy & my insurance in order to get a prescription filled for pain management. It causes increased stress & anxiety & delayed treatment means that you're not staying on top of your pain. Then you hurt all over again even worse.  Then it may take a few higher doses to get back to the manageable levels. 🤦🤦🤦
